 - Development of a sparse NLP solver and associated sparse NLP interface
 - Update of the mixed dense-sparse NLP solver to support full GPU compute mode
 - Unit testing and documentation were expanded and consolidated
 - Added partial support for device/GPU computations for the linear algebra of sparse NLPs
 - Second-order corrections to the full-Newton search directions
 - Support for the relaxing and adjustment of variables and constraints bounds
 - Implemented gradient-based scaling of the problem
 - Least-squares initialization and computation of the duals
 - Support for inertia computation and regularization for KKT linearizations systems

using real_type             = double;

Fix erroneous reading of HDF5 files

There was an error in the HDF5 read routine. I erroneously assumed that
the global arrays w, z, p, ... had the same LM numbering scheme as the
corresponding local arrays w_LMloc, z_LMloc, p_LMloc, etc., i.e. that
just w_LMloc == w(llm:ulm, :).

Therefore I assumed I could just call the HDF5 read routine on rank 0
with the global arrays instead of the local arrays and they would be
filled correctly.

Fixed by always reading the local arrays (for which the HDF5 routines
are meant to be used) and doing appropriate

   call gather_from_lo_to_rank0(w_LMloc(llm:,nR),w(1,nR))
   ...

calls that gather the local information back to task 0.

Of course, in the long run these global arrays should be eliminated
anyway, which is why I chose to do it this way instead of creating a
specific HDF5 read routine for the global arrays on rank 0, which would
avoid these MPI calls.

Perfect conductor boundary conditions (top & bottom)

This implementation has been proposed by Domenico Meduri and Laurene Jouve.

It is similar to the implementation that is currently used in the ASH code.

To deal with the over-constraint on the poloidal component, the condition

(1) Br=0 ==> B_p = 0

is applied at the boundaries n_r=(1,n_r_max) and the condition on the current

(2) n x j= 0

is applied in the domain n_r=(2,n_r_max-1).

In some cases, this compromise can be more stable than just relaxing
the constraint (1) which is supposed to be sage only if
the initial conditions do match the boundary conditions.

See Glatzmaier, 1984, JCP, 55, 461

" [...] as pointed out by P. H. Roberts (private communication),
only the second [...] of these are required since the first automatically
vanishes at the bottom when u, and B, vanish there due to the radial
component of the induction equation assuming Blm was initially zero [...] "

Perfect conductor boundary conditions (top & bottom)

This implementation has been proposed by Domenico Meduri and Laurene Jouve.

It is similar to the implementation that is currently used in the ASH code.

To deal with the over-constraint on the poloidal component, the condition

(1) Br=0 ==> B_p = 0

is applied at the boundaries n_r=(1,n_r_max) and the condition on the current

(2) n x j= 0

is applied in the domain n_r=(2,n_r_max-1).

In some cases, this compromise can be more stable than just relaxing
the constraint (1) which is supposed to be sage only if
the initial conditions do match the boundary conditions.

See Glatzmaier, 1984, JCP, 55, 461

" [...] as pointed out by P. H. Roberts (private communication),
only the second [...] of these are required since the first automatically
vanishes at the bottom when u, and B, vanish there due to the radial
component of the induction equation assuming Blm was initially zero [...] "

Perfect conductor boundary conditions (top & bottom)

This implementation has been proposed by Domenico Meduri and Laurene Jouve.

It is similar to the implementation that is currently used in the ASH code.

To deal with the over-constraint on the poloidal component, the condition

(1) Br=0 ==> B_p = 0

is applied at the boundaries n_r=(1,n_r_max) and the condition on the current

(2) n x j= 0

is applied in the domain n_r=(2,n_r_max-1).

In some cases, this compromise can be more stable than just relaxing
the constraint (1) which is supposed to be sage only if
the initial conditions do match the boundary conditions.

See Glatzmaier, 1984, JCP, 55, 461

" [...] as pointed out by P. H. Roberts (private communication),
only the second [...] of these are required since the first automatically
vanishes at the bottom when u, and B, vanish there due to the radial
component of the induction equation assuming Blm was initially zero [...] "

Set ITK to be single threaded in the characterize_data script.

The characterize_data script uses multi-processing for
concurrency. ITK filters use multi-threading as part of each process. There
is the potential for contention when too many threads are created as
compared to the number of available cores on the CPU. The solution
here is to set ITK to run in single threaded mode and the speedup is
obtained from the parallel processes.

Replaced calls to GetPixelIDValue with GetPixelID.

The GetPixelIDValue returns the internal value of the enumerated type
returned by GetPixelID. The correct approach is to use the enumerated
type (in R GetPixelID will return a string, the enumerated
type, and GetPixelIDValue will return the integer value).

Addressing issues with DICOM photometric interpretation.

ITK changed the way it read images with photometric interpretation
that indicates color images (e.g. YBR_FULL_422). Instead of loading
the raw channels as vector pixels, they are now converted to RGB.

interpretation of MONOCHROME1 (minimum value displayed as white). ITK
loads the image as is, and the user needs to invert it for display.

handles the special case of `MaxUniqInpIds` with a safe static index
into `table_q`.

axi_lite_to_apb: Make pipeline registers optional

Rationale: The conversion from AXI-Lite to APB is fairly simple both for
requests and responses.  Thus, unless this needs to be clocked at very
high frequencies, it should be possible without a pipeline register.
This saves one cycle of latency for each request and one for each
response.  Since latency is presumably more critical for this conversion
that achieving maximum frequency, the default is changed to not insert
pipeline registers.

The registers cannot be completely omitted, however, because the
implementation relies on a default-ready behavior both for requests and
responses.  Fall-through registers, which are designed exactly for
adding the default-ready behavior, are thus instantiated when pipelining
is disabled.

reached its maximum number of transactions.  Prior to this fix,

maximum (that is, while `MaxTrans` read transactions were outstanding).

dependency between reads and writes.  The integrity of data or
transactions was not affected by this problem.

axi_demux: Break combinatorial simulation loop

Combinatorial processes without explicit XXX can cause circular
dependencies which causes simulators to endlessly reschedule
a loop.  Different tools have different heuristics for detecting
this and breaking up loops.  This isn't an exact science, but the
following changes seems to avoid an endless loop under Vivado XSim.

Note: There is a small behavioural change in the code:

If `ax_valid` is asserted while `ax_select >= NoMstPorts` (where `x`
is `r` or `w`), the behaviour is undefined.  In the old code this would
just not assert the `ax_ready` flag.  This is only an issue if
`ax_select` for some reason gets out of bound, which probably causes
other issues.

On the upside, the new code likely uses slightly less logic.  If the
old behaviour is required, a check to see that the select signal is
in range could be added.  Alternatively, this could be added as an
assertion.

Global abatement using direct assignment.

This commit reduces the number of global variables by creating a single
global object `afqb` to hold all of the other previous global variables
as parameters. `afqb` has the following families of properties:

- afqb.plots: Stores variables for 2D plots, assigned mostly in
  tract-details.js
- afqb.table: Stores variables for the metadata table, assigned mostly
  in sortable-table.js
- afqb.three: Stores variables for the 3D brain visualization, assigned
  mostly in 3d-brain.js
- afqb.queues: Stores all of the async queues used by the app

versions appended the mean lines to trLines and asked d3 to update the
svg line elements for all of the data in trLines. While d3 is good about
reducing work using the enter(), update(), and exit() sets, we already

can avoid checking all of the lines in trLines entirely. The subject
lines are updated only when the user updates the plot type (e.g. fa or
md). Otherwise, only the mean lines are updated. On Adam's 2013 macbook
pro this reduced the update-on-sort times from approximately 1.5 seconds
to 0.6 seconds.

- 'options' is removed from OperatorInterface.apply_inverse

- 'solver_options' is added to OperatorInterface

If not 'None', solver_options is a dict which can contain the keys
'inverse' and 'jacobian'. The following rules apply:

- OperatorInterface.apply_inverse uses the 'inverse' entry
  of solver_options for solver selection and configuration.
  If not available, or 'None', defaults are used.
- OperatorInterface.jacobian uses the values of the 'jacobian'
  entry of solver_options as solver_options for the Jacobian
  operator. If missing, solver_options is set to None.
- OperatorInterface.assemlbe returns an assembled operator with
  the same solver_options.
- OperatorInterface.projected and OperatorInterface.restricted
  return operators with solver_options set to None.

Merge pull request #1304 from pymor/qt_vis_improv

This PR contains various improvements to make the Qt-based visualizations more reliable:

- Qt.py is replaced by qtpy, which seems more common (it originates from spyder, which our users often use) and seems to be able to detect if Qt bindings are already loaded (and uses these). The preferred bindings can be selected using QT_API which is respected by IPython as well.
- The old forking mechanism (which never worked on windows) to allow non-blocking visualizations has been removed.
- When running under IPython, the `%gui qt` magic is now used to allow non-blocking visualization.
- As a fallback, a new `pymor-viz` script has been added which shows pickled visualization data. If non-blocking visualization is requested and IPython is unavailable, this script is used.
- The code for non-blocking visualization can also be specified by setting the new `builtin.gui.qt.background_visualization_method.method` default (ipython_if_possible, ipython, pymor-vis).
- The quirks for matplotlib backend selection (in particular forcing the deprecated qt4agg backend on windows) have been removed.

Further, to make the `pymor-demo` and `pymor-vis` scripts usable on windows, these scripts have been moved to the new `pymor.scripts` subpackage, and we now use the `entry_points` mechanism to launch them

*Note:* IPython only spins Qt's event loop when waiting for input. In a long-running script, you will only see results, after the script is complete, even when executed with IPython. In that case, the pymor-vis backend might be preferable.

[operators] add 'assemble' and '_assemble_lincomb' to OperatorInterface

This commit introduces several changes to the operator interface:

- Every operator has to provide an 'assemble' method returning
  a non-parametric assembled operator. What 'assembled' means, is
  up to the given operator. OperatorBase implements 'assemble' by
  returning a FixedParameterOperator.
- AssemblableOperator is gone. Caching for non-parametric operators
  is now implemented in NumpyMatrixBasedOperator. If the operator
  is parametric, the result of '_assemble' will, however, not be
  remembered by the operator.
- The default implementation of 'lincomb' in OperatorBase now always
  returns a LincombOperator.
- The 'assemble' method of LincombOperator calls '_assemble_lincomb'
  on the first of its operators, after assembling each these operators.
  As a consequence, NumpyLincombMatrixOperator is obsolete and the
  assembly code is moved to '_assemble_lincomb' of NumpyMatrixOperator.
- NumpyMatrixBasedOperator now expects '_assemble' to return a NumPy
  matrix, which is then automatically wrapped by the 'assemble' method.

linear (and in future nonlinear, least-squares) solvers of the various
opertor types in pyMOR. Currently, only the keys 'numpy_dense',
'numpy_sparse' and 'generic' are recognized.

As a rule of thumb, new operators obtained from a given operator
(projection, Jacobian, linear combination) inherit its solver_options.
Each Operator implementation should take 'solver_options' as an __init__
argument in order to being able to customize the solver options for
different operators.

[core] new mechanism for handling defaults in pyMOR

This commit introduces the new pymor.core.defaults module, replacing the
old pymor.defaults module.

The new defaults handling mechanism works as follows: From now on, each
default in pyMOR is associated to a keyword argument (with default value) of
some function:

from pymor.core.defaults import defaults

@default('tol')
def fancy_algorithm(x, y, tol=1e-10):
    return x + y + tol

If fancy_algorithm is contained in package.module, a new user-modifiable
default 'package.module.fancy_algorithm.tol' with value '1e-10' is added
to pyMOR's global default registry (pymor.core.defaults._default_container).

fancy_algorithm will behave as follows:

fancy_algorithm(0, 0) == 1e-10
fancy_algorithm(0, 0, None) == 1e-10
fancy_algorithm(0, 0, 42) == 42

The special behaviour for 'None' allows the following design pattern:

def solve_something(x, tol_for_fancy_algorithm=None):
   ...
   r = fancy_algorithm(x, x, tol=tol_for_fancy_algorithm)
   ...

Defaults can be viewed and modified using the print_defaults,
set_defaults, load_defaults_from_file and write_defaults_to_file
methods. Defaults are auto-loaded from a pymor_defaults.py in your
current working directory. (You can also define the PYMOR_DEFAULTS
environment variable.)

The set of all default values should be considered to be the only global
state there is in pyMOR which affects computations. The state of the
default values is now included in every state id which is calculated.
The result of any (mathematically relevant) method call on an immutable
object is therefore fully determined by the following data:

  the state id of the object, the arguments to the function call,
  the current state of the global defaults

(As immutable objects are not completely immutable in pyMOR, see, e.g.,
pymor.operators.basic.NumpyMatrixBasedOperator, this is actually only a
very strong convention.)

For further details, see the documentation of pymor.core.defaults.

This commit also updates pyMOR to use the new defaults mechanism. This
leads to the following minor changes:

- The default log levels is now also a default associated to the new
  pymor.core.logger.set_log_levels method.
- A default random seed is attached to the new
  pymor.tools.random.new_random_state method, which creates a new
  numpy.random.RandomState. Each method in pyMOR using random numbers
  should from now on always operate on either a user-provided random
  state or a random state created via this method. (This eliminates
  the states of the Python and NumPy random generators from the relevant
  global state.) See pymor.parameters.spaces.CubicParameterSpace.sample_randomly
  for an example.
- Addition of pymor.tools.pprint containing 'format_array' which is used
  by Parameter.__str__
- New behaviour of float_cmp: atol is no longer set to rtol if atol is
  None. Both atol and rtol are now pyMOR defaults.
- pymor.la.numpysolvers now contains all the code involved with linear
  solvers for NumPy matrices.

Replace all Cython modules by equivalent NumPy code (#1314)

This PR replaces all existing Cython modules by NumPy code. `inplace.pyx` is simply replaced by `numpy.add.at` and `numpy.subtract.at` which were added in NumPy 1.8. For `compute_edges` I expect similar performance of the new NumPy code in comparison to the Cython code. The new implementation of `inverse_relation` is significantly slower, however. On my machine, the following code requires around 30s for `inverse_relation`, whereas the Cython version only requires 2.6s. However, this is for a grid with 40 million entities.

```python
from pymor.basic import *
from pymor.discretizers.builtin.relations import inverse_relation
from time import perf_counter
SE = TriaGrid((10000, 1000)).subentities(0, 2)
tic = perf_counter()
SUE, SUI = inverse_relation(SE, with_indices=True)
print(len(SE), perf_counter() - tic)
```

The effort scales with the mesh size. For a more realistic `TriaGrid` with 4 million entities the effort is 3s vs 0.26s. `inverse_relation` mainly is used in the `Grid` interface to compute the `superentities` of an entity. However, the result is `cached`, and assembling `Operators` over the grid should be more expensive. A second use is in `flatten_grid`, which is used by our visualizers to handle `Grids` with periodic boundaries. Overall, the benefits of having a pure Python package significantly outweighs this issue, IMHO.

Provide a default implementation of apply_inverse by converting to a NumPy/SciPy matrix (#1662)

As a fallback for operators which do not implement their own linear solvers, `Operator.apply_inverse` calls out to an unpreconditioned LGMRES, which usually fails to converge.

As a better alternative, we now try to first convert the operator to a `NumpyMatrixOperator` by calling `to_matrix`, converting the `source` and `range` arrays via `to_numpy`/`from_numpy`. This is useful, for instance, if one has to deal with `BlockOperators` of `NumpyMatrixOperators`. If this approach fails, the LGMRES fallback is still used.

Additionally, when these default implementations are used, a warning is now logged. The warning can be silenced by explicitly specifying `to_matrix` or `generic_lgmres` as the solver in `solver_options`.

created a new hash function to make Mu values hashable. This function does the following

- value of a key is by design choice a NumPy array, which is mutable and unhashable. tuple(value) turns it into a hashable tuple.
- Then we make a list of (key, value_tuple) pairs.
- We sort the key_value_tuple list for consistency, because dictionaries do not guarantee order. Sorting ensures that the hash is always the same regardless of the order of a dictionary.
- Finally we convert the sorted list to a tuple (which is hashable) and compute the hash.

[la] add VectorSpaces to  VectorArrayInterface

This commit introduces the concept of VectorSpaces to pyMOR.
This involves the following changes:

- VectorArrayInterface gains a 'subtype' property. Two arrays
  are compatible if they are of the same type and subtype.
  (Think of the subtype as, e.g., dimension or a socket for
  communication with a particular PDE solver instance.)
- A 'make_array' classmethod has been added to VectorArrayInterface.
  This method is used as a factory for arrays of null vectors.
  An appropriate 'subtype' has to be provided, when calling
  'make_array'. The resulting array will be of this subtype.
  (What appropriate means, depends on the specific array
  implementation.)
- The methods 'empty' and 'zeros' of VectorArrayInterface are
  now methods (not classmethods), creating arrays of the same
  subtype as the array, they are called upon.
  NOTE: As a consequence, there is no longer an interface for
  creating VectorArrays of arbitrary dimension.
- The new VectorSpace class represents the combination of a
  VectorArrayInterface subclass with an appropriate subtype.
  This data is exactly sufficient to construct new arrays
  using new 'make_array' method. A VectorArray is contained in
  a vector space, iff it is an instance of the subclass and has
  the same subtype.
- VectorArrayInterface gains an abstract property 'space',
  returning the space of the array, i.e.
  'VectorSpace(type(self), self.subtype)'
- The 'dim_source', 'type_source', 'dim_range', 'type_range' attributes
  of OperatorInterface are replaced by 'source' and 'range'
  VectorSpaces.
- The 'dim_solution', 'type_solution' attributes of
  DiscretizationInterface are replaced by the 'solution_space'
  VectorSpace.
- For convenicence, a 'NumpyVectorSpace(dim)' method was added,
  returning VectorSpace(NumpyVectorArray, dim).

Everything in pyMOR has been updated accordingly, except for
playground.remote which at the moment is not working.

intermittent MPI CI failure workaround (#1250)

This workaround treats the result of pytest as the success/fail trigger for the pipeline
not the exit code of the mpirun script.

The background here are intermittent failures were one rank does not call `MPI_Finalize` 
before exiting. While I made it configurable for pyMOR to tell mpi4py to do that
or not on module de-init, mpirun still sometimes errors out with "unclean"
process exits. These are never reproducable (locally or on pipeline re-run), not limited to 
python versions, nor have any other descernible pattern. Which is why I propose this workaround. 

This PR also forces the mpi runtime to use the in memory transport which
should stop the "slow transport fallback" message from popping up in logs.

Moebius Transform Operator and Tustin's method for LTI-Systems (#1614)

I have this code here that I would like to integrate in order to have Bilinear Transformations of LTI-systems similarly to Matlabs `c2d` and `d2c` commands. So far I have implemented Tustin's method and I am looking to extend this to higher order approximations in the future. 

I am particularly interested in arbitrary Moebius substitutions of the frequency argument (not only the bilinear transformation) which is why I chose a more functional approach and implemented a `MoebiusTransform` operator directly. Maybe this can be used elsewhere in the future (I have added the CayleyTransform as an inspiration).

I would love to get some feedback, IMO the method `LTIModel.moebius_substitution` could use some improvement in both naming and the code. The method substitutes the frequency argument `omega` by a MoebiusTransform (please see https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/489281/ for reference). I feel like I am not using pyMORs structure optimally in the current implementation.

The docstrings are sparse and sketchy, I will obviously add proper ones and tests at a later stage.

[operators] introduce 'solver_options'

- 'options' is removed from OperatorInterface.apply_inverse
- 'invert_options' is removed from OperatorInterface
- 'solver_options' is added to OperatorInterface

If not 'None', solver_options is a dict which can contain the keys
'inverse' and 'jacobian'. The following rules apply:

- OperatorInterface.apply_inverse uses the 'inverse' entry
  of solver_options for solver selection and configuration.
  If not available, or 'None', defaults are used.
- OperatorInterface.jacobian uses the values of the 'jacobian'
  entry of solver_options as solver_options for the Jacobian
  operator. If missing, solver_options is set to None.
- OperatorInterface.assemlbe returns an assembled operator with
  the same solver_options.
- OperatorInterface.projected and OperatorInterface.restricted
  return operators with solver_options set to None.

This PR contains various improvements to make the Qt-based visualizations more reliable:

- Qt.py is replaced by qtpy, which seems more common (it originates from spyder, which our users often use) and seems to be able to detect if Qt bindings are already loaded (and uses these). The preferred bindings can be selected using QT_API which is respected by IPython as well.
- The old forking mechanism (which never worked on windows) to allow non-blocking visualizations has been removed.
- When running under IPython, the `%gui qt` magic is now used to allow non-blocking visualization.
- As a fallback, a new `pymor-viz` script has been added which shows pickled visualization data. If non-blocking visualization is requested and IPython is unavailable, this script is used.
- The code for non-blocking visualization can also be specified by setting the new `builtin.gui.qt.background_visualization_method.method` default (ipython_if_possible, ipython, pymor-vis).
- The quirks for matplotlib backend selection (in particular forcing the deprecated qt4agg backend on windows) have been removed.

Further, to make the `pymor-demo` and `pymor-vis` scripts usable on windows, these scripts have been moved to the new `pymor.scripts` subpackage, and we now use the `entry_points` mechanism to launch them

*Note:* IPython only spins Qt's event loop when waiting for input. In a long-running script, you will only see results, after the script is complete, even when executed with IPython. In that case, the pymor-vis backend might be preferable.

[operators] add 'assemble' and '_assemble_lincomb' to OperatorInterface

This commit introduces several changes to the operator interface:

- Every operator has to provide an 'assemble' method returning
  a non-parametric assembled operator. What 'assembled' means, is
  up to the given operator. OperatorBase implements 'assemble' by
  returning a FixedParameterOperator.
- AssemblableOperator is gone. Caching for non-parametric operators
  is now implemented in NumpyMatrixBasedOperator. If the operator
  is parametric, the result of '_assemble' will, however, not be
  remembered by the operator.
- The default implementation of 'lincomb' in OperatorBase now always
  returns a LincombOperator.
- The 'assemble' method of LincombOperator calls '_assemble_lincomb'
  on the first of its operators, after assembling each these operators.
  As a consequence, NumpyLincombMatrixOperator is obsolete and the
  assembly code is moved to '_assemble_lincomb' of NumpyMatrixOperator.
- NumpyMatrixBasedOperator now expects '_assemble' to return a NumPy
  matrix, which is then automatically wrapped by the 'assemble' method.

[core] new mechanism for handling defaults in pyMOR

This commit introduces the new pymor.core.defaults module, replacing the
old pymor.defaults module.

The new defaults handling mechanism works as follows: From now on, each
default in pyMOR is associated to a keyword argument (with default value) of
some function:

from pymor.core.defaults import defaults

@default('tol')
def fancy_algorithm(x, y, tol=1e-10):
    return x + y + tol

If fancy_algorithm is contained in package.module, a new user-modifiable
default 'package.module.fancy_algorithm.tol' with value '1e-10' is added
to pyMOR's global default registry (pymor.core.defaults._default_container).

fancy_algorithm will behave as follows:

fancy_algorithm(0, 0) == 1e-10
fancy_algorithm(0, 0, None) == 1e-10
fancy_algorithm(0, 0, 42) == 42

The special behaviour for 'None' allows the following design pattern:

def solve_something(x, tol_for_fancy_algorithm=None):
   ...
   r = fancy_algorithm(x, x, tol=tol_for_fancy_algorithm)
   ...

Defaults can be viewed and modified using the print_defaults,
set_defaults, load_defaults_from_file and write_defaults_to_file
methods. Defaults are auto-loaded from a pymor_defaults.py in your
current working directory. (You can also define the PYMOR_DEFAULTS
environment variable.)

The set of all default values should be considered to be the only global
state there is in pyMOR which affects computations. The state of the
default values is now included in every state id which is calculated.
The result of any (mathematically relevant) method call on an immutable
object is therefore fully determined by the following data:

  the state id of the object, the arguments to the function call,
  the current state of the global defaults

(As immutable objects are not completely immutable in pyMOR, see, e.g.,
pymor.operators.basic.NumpyMatrixBasedOperator, this is actually only a
very strong convention.)

For further details, see the documentation of pymor.core.defaults.

This commit also updates pyMOR to use the new defaults mechanism. This
leads to the following minor changes:

- The default log levels is now also a default associated to the new
  pymor.core.logger.set_log_levels method.
- A default random seed is attached to the new
  pymor.tools.random.new_random_state method, which creates a new
  numpy.random.RandomState. Each method in pyMOR using random numbers
  should from now on always operate on either a user-provided random
  state or a random state created via this method. (This eliminates
  the states of the Python and NumPy random generators from the relevant
  global state.) See pymor.parameters.spaces.CubicParameterSpace.sample_randomly
  for an example.
- Addition of pymor.tools.pprint containing 'format_array' which is used
  by Parameter.__str__
- New behaviour of float_cmp: atol is no longer set to rtol if atol is
  None. Both atol and rtol are now pyMOR defaults.
- pymor.la.numpysolvers now contains all the code involved with linear
  solvers for NumPy matrices.

Replace all Cython modules by equivalent NumPy code (#1314)

This PR replaces all existing Cython modules by NumPy code. `inplace.pyx` is simply replaced by `numpy.add.at` and `numpy.subtract.at` which were added in NumPy 1.8. For `compute_edges` I expect similar performance of the new NumPy code in comparison to the Cython code. The new implementation of `inverse_relation` is significantly slower, however. On my machine, the following code requires around 30s for `inverse_relation`, whereas the Cython version only requires 2.6s. However, this is for a grid with 40 million entities.

```python
from pymor.basic import *
from pymor.discretizers.builtin.relations import inverse_relation
from time import perf_counter
SE = TriaGrid((10000, 1000)).subentities(0, 2)
tic = perf_counter()
SUE, SUI = inverse_relation(SE, with_indices=True)
print(len(SE), perf_counter() - tic)
```

The effort scales with the mesh size. For a more realistic `TriaGrid` with 4 million entities the effort is 3s vs 0.26s. `inverse_relation` mainly is used in the `Grid` interface to compute the `superentities` of an entity. However, the result is `cached`, and assembling `Operators` over the grid should be more expensive. A second use is in `flatten_grid`, which is used by our visualizers to handle `Grids` with periodic boundaries. Overall, the benefits of having a pure Python package significantly outweighs this issue, IMHO.

Provide a default implementation of apply_inverse by converting to a NumPy/SciPy matrix (#1662)

As a fallback for operators which do not implement their own linear solvers, `Operator.apply_inverse` calls out to an unpreconditioned LGMRES, which usually fails to converge.

As a better alternative, we now try to first convert the operator to a `NumpyMatrixOperator` by calling `to_matrix`, converting the `source` and `range` arrays via `to_numpy`/`from_numpy`. This is useful, for instance, if one has to deal with `BlockOperators` of `NumpyMatrixOperators`. If this approach fails, the LGMRES fallback is still used.

Additionally, when these default implementations are used, a warning is now logged. The warning can be silenced by explicitly specifying `to_matrix` or `generic_lgmres` as the solver in `solver_options`.

created a new hash function to make Mu values hashable. This function does the following

- value of a key is by design choice a NumPy array, which is mutable and unhashable. tuple(value) turns it into a hashable tuple.
- Then we make a list of (key, value_tuple) pairs.
- We sort the key_value_tuple list for consistency, because dictionaries do not guarantee order. Sorting ensures that the hash is always the same regardless of the order of a dictionary.
- Finally we convert the sorted list to a tuple (which is hashable) and compute the hash.

[la] add VectorSpaces to  VectorArrayInterface

This commit introduces the concept of VectorSpaces to pyMOR.
This involves the following changes:

- VectorArrayInterface gains a 'subtype' property. Two arrays
  are compatible if they are of the same type and subtype.
  (Think of the subtype as, e.g., dimension or a socket for
  communication with a particular PDE solver instance.)
- A 'make_array' classmethod has been added to VectorArrayInterface.
  This method is used as a factory for arrays of null vectors.
  An appropriate 'subtype' has to be provided, when calling
  'make_array'. The resulting array will be of this subtype.
  (What appropriate means, depends on the specific array
  implementation.)
- The methods 'empty' and 'zeros' of VectorArrayInterface are
  now methods (not classmethods), creating arrays of the same
  subtype as the array, they are called upon.
  NOTE: As a consequence, there is no longer an interface for
  creating VectorArrays of arbitrary dimension.
- The new VectorSpace class represents the combination of a
  VectorArrayInterface subclass with an appropriate subtype.
  This data is exactly sufficient to construct new arrays
  using new 'make_array' method. A VectorArray is contained in
  a vector space, iff it is an instance of the subclass and has
  the same subtype.
- VectorArrayInterface gains an abstract property 'space',
  returning the space of the array, i.e.
  'VectorSpace(type(self), self.subtype)'
- The 'dim_source', 'type_source', 'dim_range', 'type_range' attributes
  of OperatorInterface are replaced by 'source' and 'range'
  VectorSpaces.
- The 'dim_solution', 'type_solution' attributes of
  DiscretizationInterface are replaced by the 'solution_space'
  VectorSpace.
- For convenicence, a 'NumpyVectorSpace(dim)' method was added,
  returning VectorSpace(NumpyVectorArray, dim).

intermittent MPI CI failure workaround (#1250)

This workaround treats the result of pytest as the success/fail trigger for the pipeline
not the exit code of the mpirun script.

The background here are intermittent failures were one rank does not call `MPI_Finalize` 
before exiting. While I made it configurable for pyMOR to tell mpi4py to do that
or not on module de-init, mpirun still sometimes errors out with "unclean"
process exits. These are never reproducable (locally or on pipeline re-run), not limited to 
python versions, nor have any other descernible pattern. Which is why I propose this workaround. 

This PR also forces the mpi runtime to use the in memory transport which
should stop the "slow transport fallback" message from popping up in logs.

Moebius Transform Operator and Tustin's method for LTI-Systems (#1614)

I have this code here that I would like to integrate in order to have Bilinear Transformations of LTI-systems similarly to Matlabs `c2d` and `d2c` commands. So far I have implemented Tustin's method and I am looking to extend this to higher order approximations in the future. 

I am particularly interested in arbitrary Moebius substitutions of the frequency argument (not only the bilinear transformation) which is why I chose a more functional approach and implemented a `MoebiusTransform` operator directly. Maybe this can be used elsewhere in the future (I have added the CayleyTransform as an inspiration).

I would love to get some feedback, IMO the method `LTIModel.moebius_substitution` could use some improvement in both naming and the code. The method substitutes the frequency argument `omega` by a MoebiusTransform (please see https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/489281/ for reference). I feel like I am not using pyMORs structure optimally in the current implementation.

The docstrings are sparse and sketchy, I will obviously add proper ones and tests at a later stage.

and a state monitor for the synapses instantiated, the pre-template prep code would identify the size of the connected sub-populations for the
srcN and trgN variables of the stateMonitorModel. These variables are then used for the argument list of the convert_dense_matrix_2_dynamic_arrays and
convert_sparse_synapses_2_dynamic_arrays calls that translate GeNN synaptic data into brian format synaptic data. Because brian2genn implements sub-populations
only by connectivity matrices between full populations, the conversion functions need the size of the full populations, not of the connected sub-populations.
I believe the srcN and trgN variables are solely for teh purpose of these conversions, so should not be needed to represent subpopulation size elsewhere.
